newsitem.title: UK: UK investors brace for Wall St open after sell-off.
newsitem.headline: UK investors brace for Wall St open after sell-off.

text.p: Britain's leading share index clawed back from a steep opening selloff on Monday as investors braced for the start on Wall Street, after the biggest one-day point drop since October 1987 rocked London and New York on Friday.
But fears of an aftershock following Friday's 22 billion pounds ($35.4 billion) share writeoff initially proved overblown, market sources said.
By 1303 GMT, the FTSE 100 was down just 24.5 points or 0.5 percent at 4,841.3 after hitting a day's low of 4,779.3.
The Dow industrials were expected to open mixed, gaining some support from higher futures and steadier bonds.

"My belief is that this is an aberration and if institutional investors take advantage of the correction to get back in, both U.S. and domestic investors, we may see a strong end to the week," said Savvas Savouri, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
Many strategists and traders said the 2.5 percent FTSE selloff on Friday was more a correction to this year's record run rather than the start of a bear market.
Expectations for UK interest rates to stay on hold for the time being, after four hikes in four months, and high cash levels among institutions were prime reasons.

Yet another sharp drop in the Dow industrials or fears of monetary tightening in the United States or continental Europe, would rattle London investors, and some warned that as much as a 10 percent correction would ensue.

London's blue-chip index gained 24 percent so far this year to its all-time best of 5,095.3 hit on August 7. Since then, it has lost 6.2 percent and Friday's drop was the largest percentage fall in five years.

"How the U.S. opens is crucial," Credit Lyonnais Laing's Savouri said. "After a 250-point fall (in the Dow industrials) you would want to see buying interest at these lower levels, and if there isn't then that will set off the alarm bells."

But there were some bullish signals as the September S&P futures contract on Globex, the after-hours electronic trading system on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, was up on Monday morning by 0.60 points at 899.40.
The weekend may also have proved more soothing than worrying, sources said, as investors had a couple of extra days to ponder the sell-off and think about the market's fundamentals.
"We've got a 4,800 year-end target and we don't expect it to move a lot from here," said Ian Scott, UK equity strategist at Lehman Brothers.
A sharp recovery in the broader market in the last two weeks -- the FTSE 250 actually ended higher on Friday-- also alleviated fears of a full-blown bear market, market sources said.
By midday Monday, the FTSE 250 was down 0.82 percent or 38.7 points at 4,659.5 after hitting a five-month high of 4,712.9 Friday.

Sterling's retreat against the German mark after the Bank of England signalled early this month that interest rates may stay on hold, has boosted the fortunes of the second-tier industrial companies with a large percentage of overseas earnings.
Those companies' profits were hit by sterling's rise as their earnings dwindle when converted from the local currency.

"I think we have seen the worse for the day and I don't think we are in a bear phase," one trader said. "This is a good healthy correction after the British and global stock markets extended themselves."
But Richard Jeffrey, head of research at Charterhouse Tilney, said the FTSE 100 could eventually fall another 400 to 500 points, or about 10 percent.
"As far as London is concerned, yes, it is New York, and the worry about interest rates having to rise sharply for the rest of the year," he said.
($ = 0.620 British Pounds)
